description: We are Elettronici in Orbita, five Electronic Engineering students at Politecnico di Milano who love space and electronics that helps people.  Outside the lab we’re into astronomy, robotics, music, hiking and the occasional coffee-fuelled all-nighter.
summary:
We designed and simulated a compact system that monitors astronauts’ muscle health through surface EMG. Four simultaneous channels pick up the electrical activity of the muscle from skin electrodes. Each channel uses a low-noise instrumentation amplifier, a filter chain covering the 20–500 Hz EMG band and a gain stage. A right-leg-drive circuit cancels common-mode noise such as 50 Hz mains interference. A 24-bit simultaneous-sampling ADC digitizes all channels at the same instant and sends the data over SPI to an ESP32, which filters the signal and streams it to our monitoring software. On the software side, a browser-based console receives the data in real time and shows it on an interactive anatomical map. For each muscle, it compares every session with the astronaut’s own Day 1 baseline and flags it as nominal, warning or critical based on absolute thresholds, percentage loss and consecutive daily drops.

This addresses the challenge by turning raw sensor data into an early, personalized indicator of muscle deterioration, instead of relying on weight alone. This matters because microgravity and long missions cause muscle loss, and crews cannot easily access medical care. Day-by-day monitoring lets astronauts detect problems early and consult the crew medical officer before muscle loss becomes serious.
details:
What it does and how it works

The system monitors muscle health in astronauts. A 4-channel surface EMG front-end picks up the electrical activity of the muscles. Each channel has a low-noise instrumentation amplifier, a 20–500 Hz filter chain and ~40 dB of total gain. A right-leg-drive circuit cancels common-mode noise such as mains interference. A 24-bit simultaneous-sampling ADC digitizes the four channels at the same instant and sends them over SPI to an ESP32. The ESP32 streams the signal over USB to a web console that runs in the browser on a PC, where it is cleaned with a Kalman filter. The astronaut selects a muscle on an anatomical map. The console shows where to place the electrodes and which isometric exercise to perform, then records the muscle activity for 5 s. Each session is compared with the astronaut’s own Day 1 baseline, and each muscle is classified as nominal, warning or critical using the EMG signal only. The astronaut can also log body weight, calories and protein intake. Of these, only body weight is analysed, and the console raises an alert when it drops.

Benefits and intended impact

It gives crews and ground teams an early, personalized, day-by-day indicator of muscle deterioration, instead of relying on weight alone. The system detects a slow, steady decline in a muscle even while its absolute values are still in the normal range. The software does not prescribe exercise or diet. When it flags a problem, the astronaut is prompted to consult the crew medical officer, who can act before muscle loss becomes serious on long missions. Because the console needs no server or internet connection, it can run on any onboard laptop.

Tools, hardware and software

Hardware: INA333 instrumentation amplifiers, LTC6082 op-amps, ADS131E04 ADC, ESP32-DevKitC, SRV05-4 ESD protection.

Design tools: KiCad (schematic and PCB) and LTspice (simulated band 19.9–498 Hz).

Software:

  • ESP32 firmware in C++ (Arduino). It runs without blocking and sends an amplitude value 20 times per second over USB serial at 115200 baud.
    • Web Serial API to read the data stream from the ESP32.
    • A 1D Kalman filter that smooths the noisy EMG amplitude with much less lag than a moving average. At each sample, it weighs the new measurement against the previous estimate, based on the expected sensor noise and how fast the muscle signal can change.
    • Chart.js for the live oscilloscope and the multi-day trend charts.
    • An interactive SVG anatomical map with 12 muscle groups, coloured by their latest status.
    • A long-term EMG diagnostic algorithm.
    • A body-weight log with automatic alerts (warning below −2.5%, critical below −5% from baseline).
    • Calorie and protein logging.
    • localStorage for the per-astronaut history.
  • A stand-alone mode with a reference signal allows demos and tests without the board.

Creativity

We treat muscle loss as a trend problem, not a single measurement. Surface EMG is usually used in rehabilitation and sports; here it becomes a long-term health marker for astronauts. The diagnostic algorithm combines three criteria:

  1. absolute thresholds (below 3.05 mV is warning, below 2.00 mV is critical; currently calibrated on simulated data),
  2. the percentage change from the astronaut’s own Day 1 baseline (−12% is warning, −25% is critical),
  3. a slope check that raises a warning after two consecutive daily drops.

A muscle that is still “normal” in absolute terms can therefore be flagged early, if it is declining compared to that person’s own history. The hardware is original too: a four-channel analog front-end designed from scratch, with a shared right-leg-drive loop and a simultaneous-sampling 24-bit ADC, on a compact board powered from a single 3.3 V supply.

Factors considered

Signal quality came first, because EMG signals are only millivolts. Before building anything, we designed and validated the whole analog chain in LTspice, simulating the filters, gain and frequency response so that the board is right by design, not by trial and error. An instrumentation amplifier with high common-mode rejection reads each muscle. A right-leg-drive loop sums all four channels and feeds the common-mode signal back to the body, cancelling mains interference at its source. A 20 Hz high-pass filter removes electrode offset and motion drift, and a 500 Hz low-pass filter limits noise and prevents aliasing. We chose a single 3.3 V supply, ESD protection on every input, and low power and small size for a space mission. For the PCB layout we planned separate analog and digital sections and shielding of the sensitive analog paths.

On the software side:

  • Repeatable measurements. The guided procedure (electrode placement and isometric exercise) makes sessions comparable across days.
  • Real-time display. The Kalman filter gives a clean signal with much less lag than a moving average, and the live chart has animations disabled to stay smooth.
  • Safety-first rules. The decision rules check the critical case first.
  • Medical decisions stay with a human. The system flags problems and refers the astronaut to the crew medical officer; it does not make treatment decisions.
  • Isolation. Running entirely in the browser with local storage avoids any dependence on network connections, which matters on a spacecraft.

Future developments

  • Nutrition in the analysis. Use calorie and protein intake together with the EMG signal, to separate muscle loss caused by low training from loss caused by poor nutrition.
  • A combined index. Merge EMG, body weight and nutrition into a single physical-condition index.
